nameStory: The Western Tanager gets its name from its western North American range, where it's a common breeding bird of mountain forests. The word 'tanager' comes from the Tupi word 'tangará,' which Portuguese explorers used for these colorful tropical birds they encountered in South America.
description: The Western Tanager is a robin-sized songbird that's quite the rare treat in New England! Males are absolutely stunning with bright yellow bodies, black wings, and orange-red heads during breeding season. Females are more subdued in yellow-green with darker wings. These medium-sized birds are about 6-7 inches long and are actually members of the cardinal family, despite their tropical tanager appearance.

idTips.label: Male breeding colors
idTips.description: Brilliant yellow body with contrasting jet-black wings and tail, topped with an orange-red head that looks almost like it's glowing in sunlight

idTips.label: Wing bars
idTips.description: Two distinct white or pale yellow wing bars that stand out boldly against the black wings, visible even when the bird is perched

idTips.label: Female coloration
idTips.description: Olive-yellow to grayish-green overall with darker wings and the same distinctive wing bars as males, much more subdued but still recognizable

idTips.label: Song
idTips.description: A hoarse, robin-like song with a scratchy quality - sounds like a robin with a sore throat singing short phrases

idTips.label: Bill shape
idTips.description: Thick, sturdy bill typical of the cardinal family, noticeably more robust than the thin bills of true tanagers

habitat: In New England, Western Tanagers are extremely rare vagrants that might appear in mature deciduous or mixed forests, especially during migration. When they do show up, look for them in oak-maple forests, wooded parks, or along forest edges where they can find insects and fruits.

seasonality.spring: Extremely rare vagrant during spring migration (May-June). Any Western Tanager sighting would be major news for local birders and worth reporting immediately.
seasonality.summer: Virtually never seen in New England during breeding season. Any summer sighting would be extraordinary and should be documented with photos.
seasonality.fall: Slightly more likely than spring but still exceptionally rare during fall migration (August-September). Young birds and females in duller plumage are most likely.
seasonality.winter: Not expected in New England winters. Any winter sighting would be a once-in-a-lifetime event requiring immediate documentation.

funFact: Western Tanagers get their fiery orange-red head color not from their genes, but from eating insects that have fed on specific plants containing red pigments - without this special diet, their heads would stay yellow!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with the much more common Scarlet Tanager, but male Western Tanagers have yellow (not red) bodies and distinctive white wing bars. Female Western Tanagers are yellower than female Scarlet Tanagers and also show those telltale wing bars.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'tanager,' this bird was recently reclassified into the cardinal family along with other North American tanagers. True tanagers are tropical birds in a completely different family, so the name is a bit of a historical mix-up that stuck.
compareHints: Western Tanagers are easily distinguished from Scarlet Tanagers by their yellow (not red) bodies and prominent white wing bars. Summer Tanagers are entirely red (males) or yellow-orange (females) without the black wings and wing bars that make Western Tanagers so distinctive.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Scarlet tanagers are the only Piranga tanager regularly found in New England, though summer tanagers occasionally wander north.
Summer tanagers are the only all-red Piranga tanager - scarlet tanagers have black wings and tails, while western tanagers show yellow and black markings.
Hepatic tanagers are much darker red than scarlet tanagers and have pale bills versus dark bills.
